# Guttilajātaka (Ja 243)

**ID:** Ja 243
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Guttilajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Musician Guttila
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja243
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Guttilajātaka* (Ja 243, PTS J II 252ff) is a canonical Jātaka narrative set in the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*), delivered by the Buddha concerning Devadatta [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879; Readings from the Jatakas]. The narrative illustrates the supremacy of Benares in musical education in ancient India [Scharfe 2002]. In the past, the Bodhisatta was born in Benares as Guttila, a master musician renowned across Jambudīpa who cared for his blind parents [Readings from the Jatakas]. His ungrateful pupil Mūsila of Ujjeni challenged him to a musical competition, seeking to surpass him [Readings from the Jatakas]. Sakka—a past incarnation of Anuruddha—intervened on Guttila's behalf by producing celestial dancing maidens to accompany Guttila's seven-stringed lute playing [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Readings from the Jatakas]. Sakka subsequently escorted Guttila to the heavenly world, where Guttila played for celestial nymphs and questioned them regarding the meritorious deeds that led to their rebirths in heaven [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), Mūsila is identified with Devadatta, Sakka with Anuruddha, the king of Benares with Ānanda, and Guttila with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879; Readings from the Jatakas].

Curated cross-references and textual analyses show a strong relationship between this Jātaka and the *Khuddakanikāya* poetry of the *Vimānavatthu*. The *Guttilavimānavatthu* (Vv 33) shares verses directly with the *Guttilajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Kingsbury 2002; von Hinüber 1996]. Machine analysis by DharmaNexus corroborates this, showing substantial internal text reuse with Vv 33 (especially across segments §0.4–2.4 and §1.0.1–2.4) and its commentary, the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Oskar von Hinüber notes that the commentator Dhammapāla appears to have developed the *Vimānavatthu* commentary on Vv 33 directly from the narrative found in the Jātaka collection [von Hinüber 1996]. Furthermore, the narrative of the *Guttilajātaka* served as the direct basis for prominent post-canonical vernacular literature in Sri Lanka, most notably the 15th-century classical Sinhala poem *Guttila Kāvya* [Holt et al. 2003; Chandawimala Thero].
